##### Observation 4850: stage verse-reading, tag answered-no-flag, status withdrawn, deleted 1

- strong: H1245; window: meaning; created_at: 2026-09-18T11:34:32Z; updated_at: 2026-09-23T08:55:03Z
- **obs_text:** Primary Hebrew term is baqash (H1245), root meaning 'to seek, require, desire, exact, request' -- showing an active volitional pursuit rather than passive reception.

**Supports (2 nodes, by verse in Scripture order):**

- **1Sa 20:1**: Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, “ What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?”
  - node 6042; word `seeks`; `H1245 בָּקַשׁ ba.qash "to seek"`; role -; disposition -; cluster M83/A_general_seeking; elsewhere in this report
- **Ecc 8:17**: then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
  - node 6181; word `find`; `H1245 בָּקַשׁ ba.qash "to seek"`; role -; disposition -; cluster M83/A_general_seeking; in this section

##### Observation 5056: stage verse-reading, tag answered-no-flag, status withdrawn, deleted 1

- strong: H1245; window: meaning; created_at: 2026-09-18T11:39:18Z; updated_at: 2026-09-23T08:55:03Z
- **obs_text:** The full vocabulary arc for baqash runs from mundane request (Esth.2.15, asking for nothing), through intellectual/existential search (Eccl.8.17), relational-devotional pursuit (Ps.27.8, Isa.65.1), to violent pursuit of a life (Jer.11.21, 37.7 context, 38.16, 44.30) -- showing the term's range covers virtually all objects of human desire and pursuit, benign to hostile.

**Supports (1 nodes, by verse in Scripture order):**

- **Ecc 8:17**: then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
  - node 6190; word `find`; `H1245 בָּקַשׁ ba.qash "to seek"`; role -; disposition -; cluster M83/A_general_seeking; in this section

##### Observation 5061: stage verse-reading, tag no-direct-connection, status draft, deleted 0

##### Observation 14224: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132448_748-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

- **obs_text:** How it co-exists: Isolation. "He has put my brothers far from me … My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me" (19:13–14). "Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

- **obs_text:** 3. (a) Why the verses were not narrated: The reason is the same as for M47. The M25 units read the life and death words. The desire side of each verse was left for this strand. The M25 ledgers often quote the verse in full, but they quote it for its life or death word: Psa 34:12, "desires life", is quoted for "long days" (LD-101).; Joh 4:14, "never be thirsty again", is quoted for "living water" (LD-121).; Ecc 5:18, "find enjoyment", is quoted for "life enjoyed, as given" (LD-115). That ledger line was woven into Ch 2. 10.6 gained Ecc 2:24–26 in the M47 pass, but not the three verses that say the same thing (3:12; 5:18; 8:15).; Three verses (Exo 14:12, Psa 34:12, Pro 8:35–36) also have a Ch 2 side. I first treated Ch 2 as closed to them. That was my over-reading of OT-08, corrected in §6.

##### Section 196: chapter 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, Planning

> ## Planning
> 
> A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.
> 
> The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.
> 
> **Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).
> 
> The same weighing is praised in an ordinary life. The woman of Proverbs 31 *"rises while it is yet night"* (31:15). *"She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard"* (31:16). The verb for considering is a planning verb. She weighs it, and then she acts.
> 
> When something has happened that no one has seen before, the first call is to weigh it before acting. After the outrage at Gibeah, *"all who saw it said, 'Such a thing has never happened or been seen … consider it, take counsel, and speak'"* (Judges 19:30).
> 
> **Planning without knowing.** The fullest picture of planning ahead in these verses is a voyage. Paul warned the crew: *"I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss"* (Acts 27:10). They listened to the pilot and the owner instead (27:11). The plan that followed is worded with all its uncertainty:
> - *"the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (27:12)
> - *"Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor"* (27:13)
> - after the storm, *"they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (27:39)
> 
> *"on the chance that somehow"*, *"supposing"*, *"if possible"*: Luke records the planners' own sense that they could not see far. The first plan was undone by the wind (Acts 27:14). The last was undone by a reef they had not seen (27:41).
> 
> Paul plans the same way, and says so. *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Romans 1:13). His intending was real and often repeated, and something outside him held it back. James says what such planning should sound like: *"If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that"* (James 4:15; see *Life and death set before a person*).
> 
> Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them.
> - At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20).
> - With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21).
> - With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7).
> - In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32).
> - Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17).
> - Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13).
> - A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7).
> The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.
> 
> **A plan carries a person's word.** When Paul changed his travel plans, he was charged with being unreliable, and he answers with the inner question: *"Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' at the same time?"* (2 Corinthians 1:17). He rests his answer on God: *"As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No"* (1:18). In this passage, a plan is something said to others. When it changes, the change can be read as a divided heart.
> 
> **Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree.
> - Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39).
> - Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).
> 
> **Planning for another's good.** Darius *"planned to set him over the whole kingdom"* (Daniel 6:3), and the verse gives the reason: *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*. The plan for Daniel at once stirred others to look for a fault in him (6:4).
> 
> A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).
> 
> **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5).
> - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*.
> - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10).
> - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place.
> - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh.
> - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2).
> - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).
> 
> **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).
> 
> **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end.
> - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9).
> - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10).
> - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39).
> - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war.
> - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth.
> - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.
> 
> The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).
> 
> Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).
> 

##### Section 259: chapter 10.13 Anger, What it rises at

> ### What it rises at
> 
> Human anger in the verses is often set off by something perceived. Sometimes the verse names hearing or seeing; sometimes the setting gives the cause.
> - **A report:** Potiphar's anger rose on his wife's words (Genesis 39:19). It was not tested, and it was false.
> - **A sight:** "when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath" (Esther 5:9).
> - **A demand, an expectation or a slight.** Rachel demanded children, and "Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in the place of God?'" (Genesis 30:2). Naaman: "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me" (2 Kings 5:11). Queen Vashti refused to come, and the king's "anger burned within him" (Esther 1:12).
> - **A rival's honour:** the women sang of David's ten thousands, and "Saul was very angry" (1 Samuel 18:8). The elder brother heard the music for his returned brother, "was angry and refused to go in" (Luke 15:28).
> - **A wrong done to another.** Jacob's sons were indignant "because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). David burned at the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:5). Nehemiah: "I was very angry when I heard their outcry" (Nehemiah 5:6). Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16).
> - **Good done,** where it breaks a rule: the ruler of the synagogue was "indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath" (Luke 13:14).
> - **A word that exposes.** At Nazareth, "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath" (Luke 4:28). At Stephen's speech, "they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:57).
> - **Being outwitted through someone close.** Samson's riddle was got out of him through his wife's tears (Judges 14:15–17; 10.10). When the men of the city answered it, he said, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle" (14:18). The Spirit rushed upon him for the striking at Ashkelon, and then, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (14:19). "And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man" (14:20).
> - **Something within.** "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1).
> 
> Whether what sets it off is true is part of the account. Potiphar acted on a lie. The officials raged at Jeremiah over a charge he denied: "It is a lie; I am not deserting" (Jeremiah 37:14). The disciples were indignant at the waste of ointment (Matthew 26:8). Mark says the indignation was first said "to themselves", then spoken, with the poor as its reason: "'Why was the ointment wasted like that? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.' And they scolded her" (Mark 14:4–5). Jesus answered, "she has done a beautiful thing to me" (Matthew 26:10), and put the poor back in their own hands: "For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them" (Mark 14:7).
> 
> Anger can rise at a charge against one's own leadership. When Dathan and Abiram accused him of making himself a prince over them, "Moses was very angry and said to the Lord, 'Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them'" (Numbers 16:15). He took the anger to the Lord. Fury can also drive authority received from others: "I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests", and "in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities" (Acts 26:10–11; 10.7).
> 
> Anger can rise at contempt for a request that rested on good done. David's men asked Nabal for "whatever you have at hand", and gave the ground: "your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm" (1 Samuel 25:7–8). Nabal answered, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?" (25:10). David said, "Every man strap on his sword!" (25:13). I have not yet read the rest of the chapter, where Abigail meets him.
> 
> Anger can rest on a misreading and still decide. When the king came back from the garden, Haman "was falling on the couch where Esther was", begging for his life, and the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" (Esther 7:8). When the gallows had done its work, "the wrath of the king abated" (7:10).
> 

##### Section 370: chapter 10.14 Humility, Jesus

> ## Jesus
> 
> In the New Testament, humility rests on what the verses say of Jesus. God's own part is in 13.1, *Lowering himself*. Here is what it means for the one who humbles himself.
> 
> **He is lowly.** "learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29). His own word on his own heart. Rest is found by learning from it.
> 
> **He came humble.** "your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey" (Matthew 21:5; Zechariah 9:9). As a boy who knew "I must be in my Father's house", "he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them" (Luke 2:49, 51). "In his humiliation justice was denied him", and like a lamb he "opens not his mouth" (Acts 8:32–33).
> 
> **He humbled himself, and was exalted.** "who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him" (Philippians 2:6–9). "we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). I read the saying he taught, "whoever humbles himself will be exalted", as what is told of him.
> 
> **He is the ground of humility toward others.**
> - "Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 2:5) is the reason for "in humility count others more significant than yourselves" (2:3).
> - "leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps" (1 Peter 2:21).
> - "out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21).
> - Paul appeals "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:1).
> 
> **Others lower themselves before him.** John the Baptist: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). He says it after "I am not the Christ", and with "this joy of mine is now complete" (3:28–29). His lowering is said with joy.
> 
> **At his coming, a low estate is looked on.** Mary: "he has looked on the humble estate of his servant" (Luke 1:48). Her song goes on as Hannah's had: he scatters "the proud in the thoughts of their hearts", brings down the mighty and exalts the humble, fills the hungry and sends the rich away (Luke 1:51–53; 1 Samuel 2:7–8).

##### Section 371: chapter 10.14 Humility, The Old Testament and the New

> ## The Old Testament and the New
> 
> Everything above is in both Testaments:
> - humbling oneself before God, and God's answer
> - the proud brought low and the humble raised
> - favour to the humble
> - the lower seat
> - the meek inheriting
> - God humbling for good
> - a humbling he does not accept
> - humility beside hearing
> - the humble king
> - God lowering himself
> 
> The New Testament quotes the Old on three of them (Proverbs 3:34; Zechariah 9:9; Psalm 8:5–6).
> 
> What differs is emphasis, and one thing that is new.
> 
> - **Before God, then also toward one another.** In the Old Testament humbling is almost always before God. Kings and the people humble themselves, and the answer is wrath turned or disaster delayed. In the New, much of what is said is about humility toward one another. It always has a reason that faces God, and the answer is named as being justified, grace, and rest for the soul.
> - **The new thing: Christ.** He is the one who is lowly in heart, who humbled himself to death, and in whose mind the humble live. What God did in looking down, in his gentleness and in his breaking over a heart, the Son did in a human life. What the Old Testament said of man, "you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings … you have put all things under his feet" (Psalm 8:5–6), the letter to the Hebrews reads as "namely Jesus" (Hebrews 2:6–9).

##### Section 380: chapter 13.1 Divine, Lowering himself

> ## Lowering himself
> 
> The Lord is high, and the verses keep saying that he looks low.
> - "Who is like the Lord our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth? He raises the poor from the dust" (Psalm 113:5–7). The verb for looking far down is the one used when he brings the proud low.
> - "For though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psalm 138:6).
> - "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isaiah 57:15).
> - David: "You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your gentleness made me great" (2 Samuel 22:36; Psalm 18:35). The word rendered "gentleness" is the word for humility.
> - Over his people's unfaithfulness: "how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me" (Ezekiel 6:9).
> 
> **In the Son.** "who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him" (Philippians 2:6–9). He says of himself, "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29). He came "humble, and mounted on a donkey" (Matthew 21:5). As a boy, "he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them" (Luke 2:51). "In his humiliation justice was denied him" (Acts 8:33). He "for a little while was made lower than the angels … crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). These are the words of Psalm 8 about man, read of Jesus (Psalm 8:5). All things are put under him, and at the end "the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28).
> 
> I read the lowering that the Old Testament tells of God, looking down, dwelling with the lowly, his gentleness, his being broken over a heart, as done in the Son in a human life.
> 
> **Toward the humble and the proud.** He sees the one who humbles himself and answers: "When the Lord saw that they humbled themselves" (2 Chronicles 12:7); "Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me?" (1 Kings 21:29). He gives favour: "to the humble he gives favor" (Proverbs 3:34); "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6). He humbles to test, "to do you good in the end" (Deuteronomy 8:16). He brings the proud low, "and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" (Isaiah 2:11). He looks on a humble estate (Luke 1:48). What this means for the one who humbles himself is in 10.14.

##### Section 387: chapter 10.15 Pride, The boast

> ## The boast
> 
> A boast is what a person stands on, said aloud. The verses do not condemn boasting as such. They judge it by what it rests on.
> 
> **In oneself.** "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches" (Jeremiah 9:23). "Those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches" are told, "Truly no man can ransom another" (Psalm 49:6–7). "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring" (Proverbs 27:1); "Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off" (1 Kings 20:11). "Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give" (Proverbs 25:14). "If you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth" (James 3:14).
> 
> **Excluded.** "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8–9). "Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded" (Romans 3:27). God chose what is low "so that no human being might boast in the presence of God" (1 Corinthians 1:29). A boast is shut out because what is held was given.
> 
> **In shame.** Paul names many who "walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things" (Philippians 3:18–19). The word is "glory" (*doxa*), not the boast word. I read it as doing the boast's work, saying what a person stands on, and as turned upside down: it rests on what should shame. Paul tells it "even with tears" (3:18; 10.10). Against it he sets, "But our citizenship is in heaven", and a Savior who "will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body" (3:20–21). "Glorious" is the same word. Their glory is in their shame, and the glory awaited is his.
> 
> **Moved.** The boast is not taken away. It is turned. "But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 9:24). "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31). "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psalm 34:2). The same Greek word becomes joy: "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Romans 5:2–3).
> 
> **In weakness.** Forced to boast, Paul turns it round: "If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness" (2 Corinthians 11:30). He holds back even a true boast, "so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me" (12:6). "I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (12:9). I read this as the opposite of pride's standing: no more is claimed than is so.
> 
> **Within a measure.** "We will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us" (2 Corinthians 10:13). It matches the measure for thinking of oneself: "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Romans 12:3). And its opposite: "For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Galatians 6:3).
> 
> **Of others.** Paul's most frequent boast is in other people. "I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort" (2 Corinthians 7:4). "What is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you?" (1 Thessalonians 2:19).

##### Section 394: chapter 10.10 Relating to others, Pride over another

> ## Pride over another
> 
> Pride between people stands over someone weaker. "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor" (Psalm 10:2). "Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker" (Proverbs 17:5). "The Lord tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries" (Proverbs 15:25). Sodom's pride sat with plenty and ease, and the poor and needy were not helped (Ezekiel 16:49). It closes the heart: "They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly" (Psalm 17:10). It divides: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Galatians 5:26). And it is set against love: "'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1).
> 
> The one under it carries it: "Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud" (Psalm 123:4).
> 
> Another's pride can also be wept over. "But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (Jeremiah 13:17). Paul writes of many "of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ" (Philippians 3:18), who "glory in their shame" (3:19). He tells it with tears, and he still tells it: "keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us" (3:17).
> 
> The word for boasting turns the other way between people when the boast is in another. "I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort" (2 Corinthians 7:4). "So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men" (2 Corinthians 8:24). The whole account is in 10.15.

##### Section 8: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Life set before a person

> ## Life set before a person
> 
> Life is set before the inner being as something to choose. "I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live" (Deuteronomy 30:19). The same chapter also speaks of God's own work on the heart: "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live" (30:6). The choice is made by doing, seeking and holding on:
> - "if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the Lord" (Leviticus 18:5)
> - "Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live" (Deuteronomy 16:20)
> - "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live" (Proverbs 4:4)
> - "Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight" (Proverbs 9:6)
> - "Seek me and live" (Amos 5:4); "Seek good, and not evil, that you may live" (5:14)
> - "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4)
> 
> Long days are promised with some of the commands. "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land" (Exodus 20:12). Moses gives the law "that you may fear the Lord your God … all the days of your life, and that your days may be long" (Deuteronomy 6:2). Peter takes up a psalm: "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil" (1 Peter 3:10).
> 
> The Preacher sets another sight beside this. "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15). And he adds: "Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God" (8:12). Scripture states both. I leave them side by side.
> 
> Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
> - "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
> - "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
> - Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death.
> - "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21). James calls the tongue "a restless evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8).
> 
> The same word can be death to one and life to another. Paul says of the message he carries: "to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?" (2 Corinthians 2:16).
> 
> Some of what kills a person is named from within. "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Proverbs names more:
> - "He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray" (Proverbs 5:23)
> - "whoever hates reproof will die" (Proverbs 15:10)
> - "he who despises his ways will die" (Proverbs 19:16)
> 
> Elihu says it of those who will not hear: "if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge" (Job 36:12). Sections 10.1, 10.5 and 10.6 follow these.
> 
> God says what he wants. "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (18:32). He says it to people who had given up: "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" The answer comes at once: "turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:10–11).
> 
> The turning is a considered act, and it reaches back over the past:
> - "Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die" (Ezekiel 18:28).
> - "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (18:22).
> - It reaches back the other way too: when a righteous man turns to injustice, "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).
> - Trust can lean the wrong way: "if he trusts in his righteousness and does injustice, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered, but in his injustice that he has done he shall die" (33:13).
> 
> Another's death can be laid at a person's hand. The watchman who does not warn the wicked is told, "his blood I will require at your hand"; if he warns and is not heeded, "you will have delivered your soul" (Ezekiel 33:8–9). Section 10.10 follows that.
> 
> Section 10.7 follows the choosing, and Chapter 14 the turning.
> 
> Life can also be wrongly kept or taken by words. God condemns those who were "putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live, by your lying to my people, who listen to lies" (Ezekiel 13:19).

##### Section 29: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, After death

> ## After death
> 
> Scripture does speak of people alive before God after death, and it uses both words.
> - John sees "under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God", crying out for justice (Revelation 6:9–10).
> - Hebrews speaks of "the spirits of the righteous made perfect" (Hebrews 12:23).
> - Peter speaks of "the spirits in prison" (1 Peter 3:19).
> - And Jesus: "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).
> 
> Whether soul or spirit is used, these verses speak of people alive before God after death.
> 
> Other verses say that the dead are silent and gone:
> - "But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?" (Job 14:10)
> - "As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up; he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore" (Job 7:9–10)
> - "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 9:5). The Preacher draws the living back to the work in hand: "Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going" (9:10).
> - "For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?" (Psalm 6:5)
> - "The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any who go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)
> - "Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you?" (Psalm 88:10)
> - "For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness. The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day" (Isaiah 38:18–19)
> - Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (Psalm 49:19)
> 
> Other passages speak of the dead in Sheol as stirred and speaking. They are oracles against kings and nations.
> - In the taunt against the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4): "Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth". They say to him, "You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!" (14:9–10).
> - Over Egypt: "The mighty chiefs shall speak of them, with their helpers, out of the midst of Sheol: 'They have come down, they lie still, the uncircumcised, slain by the sword.'" Those who "spread terror in the land of the living" now "bear their shame with those who go down to the pit" (Ezekiel 32:21, 24). The trees of Eden "were comforted in the world below" at Pharaoh's fall (31:16), and Pharaoh "will be comforted for all his multitude" (32:31).
> 
> These are prophetic oracles. Jesus also tells of two men after death, and the one who is buried is aware and speaks:
> - "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side" (Luke 16:22–23).
> - He cries, "I am in anguish in this flame". Abraham answers, "Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things … but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish", and "between us and you a great chasm has been fixed" (16:24–26).
> - He asks for his five brothers, and is told, "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead" (16:28–31).
> 
> In this account the dead remember, see, ask and are answered. One is comforted and one is in anguish, and the line between them cannot be crossed. The account does not say whether it is a story Jesus tells or an event, and I do not decide it.
> 
> So Scripture speaks of the dead in more than one way. Some verses say they know nothing, do not praise and do not return. The oracles and Luke 16 speak of them as stirred and speaking, comforted or in anguish. I do not make one of these explain the other away.
> 
> And with God, the dead are carried, blessed and at rest:
> - "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side" (Luke 16:22), where "now he is comforted" (16:25)
> - "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" (Revelation 14:13)
> - David, of his dead child: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me" (2 Samuel 12:23)
> - Jesus, answering a question about the resurrection: "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38)
> - "who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:10)
> - The psalmist: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (Psalm 49:15)
> - To the man dying beside him: "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43)
> - Paul, weighing life and death: "My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account" (Philippians 1:23–24)
> - "we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). In the same chapter he says, "not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed" (5:4, in "Waited for", above). Both are stated
> - Peter: "the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does" (1 Peter 4:6)
> 
> Scripture states both. I leave them side by side.
> 
> The living are told how to deal with the dead. Inquiring of them is forbidden: there shall not be found among you "a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead" (Deuteronomy 18:11). Israel is condemned because they "ate sacrifices offered to the dead" (Psalm 106:28). Kindness to the dead is blessed. Naomi says to her daughters-in-law, "May the Lord deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me" (Ruth 1:8).

##### Section 349: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Death spoken of in more than one way

> ### Death spoken of in more than one way
> 
> So far, death is the end of the body's life. Scripture also uses the word for more than that, sometimes in one sentence. "Leave the dead to bury their own dead" (Matthew 8:22; Luke 9:60). The first "dead" are living people; the second is the man's father. Jesus does not explain the first.
> 
> The father of the son who came home says, "this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found" (Luke 15:24). He sets "dead" beside "lost", and "alive" beside "found". The son had not died in body. The word for "lost", *apollymi* ("to destroy, perish, lose"), is used of the sheep and the coin in the same chapter (15:4, 8). It is the word in "whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3:16), and in "the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10).
> 
> The verses speak of death in these ways:
> - **the body's death**: the breath taken, the return to dust (above)
> - **death in the living**: people still alive called dead (below, "Death in the living")
> - **dying *to***: a death the believer has already died, to sin and to the law (below, "Dead to sin")
> - **a death beyond death**: "the second death" (Revelation 2:11; 20:14; 21:8; below, "Life, and judgment")
> - **death as a power** that reigns and stings (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:56; "Going down to Sheol")
> - **the living made like the dead**: for fear, the guards at the tomb "became like dead men" (Matthew 28:4); John "fell at his feet as though dead" (Revelation 1:17)
> 
> The same word changes character with what it is joined to. Of the same people Paul says that they "were dead in" their trespasses (Ephesians 2:1, 5; Colossians 2:13) and that they "died to sin" (Romans 6:2, 11). Dead *in* trespasses is death under them. Dead *to* sin is a death that ends their rule: "one who has died has been set free from sin" (Romans 6:7). The word passes even to sin itself: "apart from the law, sin lies dead"; then, "when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:8–9). It is said of faith, and set beside the body: "as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead" (James 2:26). And Paul says both of one person: "although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness" (Romans 8:10).
> 
> Perishing is spoken of in the same way. Some are perishing now: "the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18); "even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing" (2 Corinthians 4:3). Paul gives a reason in one place: "because they refused to love the truth and so be saved" (2 Thessalonians 2:10). Jesus warns, "unless you repent, you will all likewise perish" (Luke 13:3). What is set against perishing is eternal life: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish" (John 10:28).

- Ezr 4:19: And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it.
- Ezr 5:17: Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter.”
- Ezr 6:1: Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored.
- Psa 64:6: They search out injustice, saying, “We have accomplished a diligent search.” For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep.
- Psa 77:6: I said, “Let me remember my song in the night; let me meditate in my heart.” Then my spirit made a diligent search:
- Psa 139:23: Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!
- Pro 2:4: if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,
- Pro 25:2: It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.
- Ecc 1:13: And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
- Ecc 7:25: I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness.
- Jer 5:1: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her.
- Jer 17:10: “ I the Lord search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds.”
- Lam 1:11: All her people groan as they search for bread; they trade their treasures for food to revive their strength. “ Look, O Lord, and see, for I am despised.”
- Eze 34:6: they wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill. My sheep were scattered over all the face of the earth, with none to search or seek for them.
- Eze 34:11: “ For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out.
- Eze 39:14: They will set apart men to travel through the land regularly and bury those travelers remaining on the face of the land, so as to cleanse it. At the end of seven months they will make their search.
- Amo 9:3: If they hide themselves on the top of Carmel, from there I will search them out and take them; and if they hide from my sight at the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them.
- Zep 1:12: At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are complacent, those who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will not do good, nor will he do ill.’
- Mat 2:8: And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “ Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him.”
- Mat 2:13: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “ Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.”
- Mat 13:45: “ Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls,
- Mat 18:12: What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray?
- Luk 2:44: but supposing him to be in the group they went a day’s journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances,
- Joh 5:39: You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,

##### Observation 3654: stage verse-reading, tag not-related-to-meaningful-word, status withdrawn, deleted 1

##### Observation 4457: stage verse-reading, tag answered-no-flag, status withdrawn, deleted 1

##### Section 50: chapter 04 The heart, The heart is hidden, and God sees it

> ## The heart is hidden, and God sees it
> 
> "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy" (Proverbs 14:10). Other people cannot fully see into it, and often its owner cannot either. But "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The word corrects a prophet. Samuel had looked on Eliab and "thought, 'Surely the Lord's anointed is before him'" (16:6). The one sent to choose formed his thought from what he saw. God is the one who "knows the secrets of the heart" (Psalm 44:21). "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). He knows the heart's leaning before it acts: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). He tests it and weighs it: "the Lord weighs the heart" (Proverbs 21:2). People try to hide what the heart holds, and Isaiah answers them: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down!" (Isaiah 29:15–16). Section 10.11 follows hiding and disclosing.
> 
> The heart can lead a person away from life itself. "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12). Paul traces being "alienated from the life of God" to "the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Death in the living") gives the setting.
> 
> The heart is tied to life and death in plain words. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense" (Proverbs 10:21). The word for "sense" there is *heart*. "Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). And what is believed in the heart is that God raised Jesus "from the dead" (Romans 10:9). Of the heart after death, I have found nothing (Chapter 2, "Soul, spirit and heart at death").

##### Section 144: chapter 10.4 Thinking, Small, passing, and wholly seen

> ## Small, passing, and wholly seen
> 
> Human thought is real, and it is also small. "The Lord — knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).
> 
> And none of it is hidden.
> - "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2).
> - "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
> - He knows the inclination before it is acted on: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21).
> - Jesus "perceived their thoughts" (Luke 5:22).
> - What is hidden will be brought out. Simeon says the child is set for a sign "so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34–35).
> 
> The same psalm that says God knows my thoughts uses the same word for his thoughts: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).
> 
> God thinks too, and his thinking is not like mine. "The Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the plea that Joab put in a woman's mouth to move David (2 Samuel 14:3), she says of God that "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Chapter 11 returns to this.

##### Section 324: chapter 13.1 Divine, Purposing

> ## Purposing
> 
> The words used for a person who plans, devises or purposes are also used of God. The verses do not give his plans as a hidden decree working out of sight. They show him forming a plan and saying it aloud, setting it against what people devise, holding it open to their turning, carrying it out, and keeping it fixed where he has sworn.
> 
> **He forms a plan and makes it known.** "Therefore hear the plan that the Lord has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman" (Jeremiah 49:20). The same words are spoken against Babylon (50:45). In both places the plan follows his question, "For who is like me? Who will summon me?" (49:19; 50:44). Of Babylon it is said that "the Lord has both planned and done what he spoke" (51:12). The verse before shows how it went forward, through other people's spirits: "The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it" (51:11). His counsel is something to be told in full. Paul counts his own innocence in not holding it back: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27).
> 
> **His devising answers what people devise.** Micah speaks first of those "who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds" (Micah 2:1), who "covet fields and seize them" (2:2). Then: "Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The verb is the same for both, and the "therefore" ties his devising to theirs. In Jeremiah his plan and theirs stand in one exchange:
> - He says: "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (Jeremiah 18:11).
> - They answer: "That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).
> 
> **He says what he intends so that people may turn, and he relents.** At the potter's house he says, "like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand" (Jeremiah 18:6). He sets out both directions:
> - "if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8)
> - "if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it" (18:10)
> 
> His intention is spoken so that it can be heard. "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them" (Jeremiah 26:3). It is written in a scroll for the same reason: "that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin" (36:3). I read these verses as saying that the hearing and turning of the people belong to what happens to the plan. The verses themselves say "it may be", and leave the outcome open.
> 
> **He also purposes and does not turn back.** "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jeremiah 4:28). The verse before it sets a limit inside the judgment: "yet I will not make a full end" (4:27). Zechariah sets a fixed purpose for disaster beside a fixed purpose for good: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zechariah 8:14–15). When he wished to show "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Hebrews 6:17). The verses say both that he relents and that he does not relent or turn back. None of them explains how the two stand together, and I leave them as they are written.
> 
> **What he purposed is carried out, and people see afterward that it was his.** "The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago" (Lamentations 2:17). "The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line" (2:8). In Zechariah the fathers looked back and recognised it: "As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us" (Zechariah 1:6).
> 
> **He has plans for welfare, and takes thought for the one in need.**
> - "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). This is said to exiles, of what will come "When seventy years are completed" (29:10).
> - "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17).
> - In the plea Joab put in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3), the wise woman of Tekoa sets God against the fact that "We must all die": "God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14).
> 
> **His plan takes in what people do against him, and does not excuse them.** "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). The plan and the guilt are in one sentence. The church, praying Psalm 2, says that those who gathered against Jesus did "whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Acts 4:28). They then ask, "grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness" (4:29). Joseph says to his brothers, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20); the same verb is used for both.
> 
> **His purpose stands before the ages and does not rest on works.**
> - "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Timothy 1:9)
> - "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11)
> - "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11)
> 
> It is made known in Christ: "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ" (Ephesians 1:9–10). It is "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (3:11). Christ is the one "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood … to show God's righteousness" (Romans 3:25).
> 
> **The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God.** Where people do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays, and his praying is matched to God's will: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:26–27). The one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. Paul does not say here what "mind" is, and I leave the word as he gives it.
> 
> **It is turned toward those who love him.** The next verse goes straight on: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28).
> 
> **A person can refuse it, or serve it.** "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luke 7:30), while the people and the tax collectors "declared God just" (7:29). "David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep" (Acts 13:36).
> 
> What these verses mean for a person is not taken up here. Each touches the inner life in its own way:
> - the plan spoken so that a person may hear and turn
> - the purpose sworn as "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul" (Hebrews 6:19)
> - "when you seek me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13)
> - "we do not know what to pray for as we ought" (Romans 8:26), the weakness the Spirit helps
> - the heart poured out "like water before the presence of the Lord" after his purpose was carried out (Lamentations 2:19)
> - "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zechariah 8:17), said straight after his own purposing for good
> 
> These belong with a person's own planning, in 10.7 (*Planning*).
> 
> **His purpose is spoken, and carried out by another.** The delight word is also used for his purpose. He is the one "who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'" (Isaiah 44:28), at the end of a line of sayings: "who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers" (44:26). Again: "declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it" (46:10–11). It is said to people told to "remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other" (46:9). And: "Who among them has declared these things? The Lord loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon" (48:14). I read "his purpose" there as the Lord's, carried out by the one he loves, as in 44:28; it can also be read as Cyrus's own pleasure. In each place the purpose is said aloud, set against idols that declare nothing, and done through a named man. What pleases him is what he will do.
> 
> **His word carries out what he purposes.** "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth" (Isaiah 55:10), "so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it" (55:11). The act is the word going out and doing its work. "Purpose" is a delight word: what he delights in, his word carries out.

##### Section 6: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Breath lent, and held by God

> ## Breath lent, and held by God
> 
> Life is held in the breath, and the breath is God's to give and to take back.
> - "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).
> - Daniel tells a king who had praised idols that he had not honoured "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways" (Daniel 5:23).
> - "If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust" (Job 34:14–15).
> - "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:29–30).
> - "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
> - "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psalm 146:4). Thinking goes when the breath goes. "Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow" (Psalm 144:4), and the Lord "knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).
> 
> People say the same of their own lives. "Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good" (Job 7:7). James asks, "What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes." He draws from it a way of speaking about tomorrow: "Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.'" (James 4:14–15). Section 10.7 follows that.
> 
> God holds both ends. "I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "The Lord kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up" (1 Samuel 2:6). When a letter asked the king of Israel to heal a man of leprosy, he tore his clothes: "Am I God, to kill and to make alive …?" (2 Kings 5:7). And between the two ends, he keeps alive:
> - "that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine" (Psalm 33:19)
> - "He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right" (Job 36:6)
> - Joseph to his brothers: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive" (Genesis 50:20)
> - Moses joins it to the fear of God: "to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive" (Deuteronomy 6:24)
> 
> The breath does more than keep a body going. "But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8). "The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all his innermost parts" (Proverbs 20:27). There the word the ESV renders "spirit" is *nəšāmâ* ("breath"). Words come out on it too. Job asks a friend, "With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?" (Job 26:4). Not everything breathed out is good: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5). Section 10.5 follows that.
> 
> The breath can fail in a person who is still alive. After his vision Daniel says, "no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me" (Daniel 10:17). Zion is pictured "gasping for breath, stretching out her hands" (Jeremiah 4:31). The psalm's last word gives the breath its purpose: "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!" (Psalm 150:6).
> 
> God gives this frailty as a reason for holding back his anger: "I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isaiah 57:16). A psalm says what the holding back did, and why: "Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psalm 78:38–39). The people lived because his wrath was not stirred. And a whole life can be felt as lived under that anger: "For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh" (Psalm 90:9). Chapter 13 follows this.
> 
> In this, humans and animals share one lot: "They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). The flood fell on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17), and "Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died" (7:22).

##### Section 18: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Soul, spirit and heart at death

> ## Soul, spirit and heart at death
> 
> At death Scripture speaks of each inner word in its own way. For the soul, it has more than one way.
> 
> **The soul.**
> - **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
> - **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
> - **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
> - **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
> - **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
> - **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).
> 
> I read the soul in these verses as the person: the one who dies, and the one who is ransomed. It is more than a part that leaves.
> 
> **The spirit.**
> - **The spirit is committed and returns.** "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:5). Jesus "yielded up his spirit" (Matthew 27:50). "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!" (Luke 23:46). Stephen: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). "The dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
> - **The body without it is dead.** "The body apart from the spirit is dead" (James 2:26).
> - **Where it goes, the Preacher leaves as a question:** "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). I leave it where he left it.
> 
> No verse sends the soul one way and the spirit another. Of the verses that name Sheol or Hades, some speak of the soul and none speaks of the spirit.
> 
> **The heart.**
> - **It stops attending.** When the wife of Phinehas heard that the ark was taken and her husband dead, the women told her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son". "But she did not answer or pay attention" (1 Samuel 4:20). Literally, she did not *set her heart*. Rachel is told almost the same words, "Do not fear, for you have another son" (Genesis 35:17).
> 
> And one thing I did not expect: **the heart can die before the body does**. When Nabal sobered up and heard how close he had come to disaster, "his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (1 Samuel 25:37–38). The heart died first; the man died ten days later. The psalmist knows a similar death in life: "I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel" (Psalm 31:12). Literally, forgotten *from the heart*.
> 
> Scripture speaks of the heart while a person lives: "madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). I have found no verse that speaks of the heart after death.

##### Observation 5224: stage verse-reading, tag answered-no-flag, status withdrawn, deleted 1

##### Observation 14269: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132448_748-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** Part 2 verses: what they add (both were B8: human vexation induced by God): Paul reads Deu 32:21 as a statement about understanding: "But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, 'I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry'" (Rom 10:19). Then "I have been found by those who did not seek me" (10:20), and "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (10:21); The induced anger is set inside God's outstretched hands. It is a provocation meant to bring them back, not only a punishment; Compare Deu 32:29, "If they were wise, they would understand this"; God troubles the nations' hearts at another's fall: "I will trouble [ka'as] the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations" (Eze 32:9), and "They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life" (32:10). The vexation God induces comes from seeing a great power fall. It is a trouble of the onlooker, and it turns to fear for one's own life.

- **obs_text:** How it co-exists: Humbling with a confession of God's justice: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "you are just" (Ezr 9:15); Humbling with the body: torn clothes and weeping (Josiah); Humbling that is partial. Rehoboam is spared destruction but made to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms" (2Ch 12:8). Bronze shields replace gold (12:10). And "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (12:14). The humbling turned the wrath, and the heart was still not set.

##### Observation 14578: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132928_870-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:35:48Z
- **obs_text:** Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud" and 32:26 "the pride of his heart". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; D v2 §9.1, §10.1, §11; pilot §2; Outside (all genuine, the bearer's own):; 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul"; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender"; 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord"; Nothing new in any single seat. What part A adds is a third kind of seat for pilot §2. The pilot has the heart that provokes (the cause) and the spirit that receives (the effect). Part A adds the heart that turns, and so turns the anger away. In these verses, and in §22, it is the human seat most often named in the context of God's anger. For the researcher: whether pilot §2 takes this as a third row.

##### Observation 14589: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0
