##### Observation 15205: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_140758_537-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T14:08:28Z
- **obs_text:** Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.
- **revisit_note:** Captured from _analytics/Clusters/M08 - pride-arrogance/m08-batch5-reading-v1-20261015.md lines 43-69 (#2305)

##### Observation 18878: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_164113_300-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:41:39Z
- **obs_text:** Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).
- **revisit_note:** Captured from _analytics/Clusters/M20 - doubt-discouragement/wa-cluster-M20-narrative-digest-v1-20261002.md lines 110-124 (#2305)

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_164719_204-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:49:06Z
- **obs_text:** (a) The fugitive hunted to death.; Verses: 1Sa 19:2; 20:5, 19, 24; 23:19, 23; 26:1; Psa 54:1 (David); Judg 9:5 (Jotham); 2Sa 17:9 (David, as Hushai pictures him); 1Ki 17:3 (Elijah); Jer 36:19 (Baruch and Jeremiah); Jos 2:16 (the spies); Jos 10:16, 17, 27 (five kings); 2Ch 22:9 (Ahaziah); Joh 8:59; 12:36 (Jesus).; Where it comes from: a stated threat to life. "Saul my father seeks to kill you" (1Sa 19:2); Abimelech "killed his brothers … But Jotham … hid himself" (Judg 9:5); "they picked up stones to throw at him" (Joh 8:59).; The feeling of the one who hides is almost never stated. What is stated is someone else's counsel to hide: Jonathan (1Sa 19:2), Rahab (Jos 2:16), the officials (Jer 36:19), and God (1Ki 17:3). In this strand the inner operation that shows is the counsellor's: foresight and concern for the other.; What it leads to: survival (Jotham; David), or capture and death (Ahaziah, "captured while hiding", 2Ch 22:9; the five kings, Jos 10:17, 27).

##### Section 122: chapter 10.2 Knowing and hearing, (opening)

> # 10.2 Knowing and hearing
> 
> Knowing belongs chiefly to the heart, as Chapter 4 showed. To pay attention is to set the heart. To understand is to have a *hearing heart*. To remember is to keep a thing in the heart. The spirit knows the self from within: "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11). The soul receives what is known as something good to taste: "knowledge will be pleasant to your soul" (Proverbs 2:10).
> 
> **Hearing is the main way in.** The ear receives, and the heart keeps it or refuses it. "All my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears" (Ezekiel 3:10). "Making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding" (Proverbs 2:2). When the heart is hard, hearing stops: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen" (Exodus 7:13). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law" (Zechariah 7:12). A crushed spirit can block hearing as well. Israel "did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery" (Exodus 6:9).
> 
> A refusal to hear can stand on a reading of the past. The survivors in Egypt told Jeremiah, "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you" (Jeremiah 44:16). Their reason was what they remembered: "For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything" (44:17–18). They had seen the ruin (44:2; 10.13, *Seen and not taken in*) and read it the other way. I read the refusal as resting on their own account of cause and effect.
> 
> What is heard moves everything inside. Rahab says, "As soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you" (Joshua 2:11). Good news works the other way: "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25). And hearing is a kind of eating: "Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food. Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live" (Isaiah 55:2–3).
> 
> Sometimes hearing is not enough, and the inner being needs to *see*. Jacob's heart went numb at the news that Joseph was alive. His spirit revived only when he saw the wagons (Genesis 45:26–27).
> 
> Understanding has a source that Scripture names in the breath: "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8; Chapter 2). And hearing God himself was a matter of life. "Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?" (Deuteronomy 4:33). Section 10.9 follows this.
> 
> **Hearing goes both ways.** The ear is the way in, and it is also where what goes out arrives. God hears what people say: "You have heard their taunts, O Lord, all their plots against me" (Lamentations 3:61). "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention and heard them" (Malachi 3:16). And refusing to hear goes with devising. "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words" (Jeremiah 6:19). Jeremiah's enemies plot against him with these words: "let us not pay attention to any of his words" (Jeremiah 18:18).
> 
> What a person listens to shows what he is: *"An evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue"* (Proverbs 17:4).
> 
> Who speaks can decide whether a word is heard. In the Preacher's example a poor, wise man "by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man. But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard" (Ecclesiastes 9:15–16). His wisdom had saved them. I read the verse as saying that what was seen in him was his poverty, and that was why he was forgotten and not heard (10.3).
> 
> Hearing can be taken away, and then wanted. *"Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord God, when I will send a famine on the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. They shall wander from sea to sea … to seek the word of the Lord, but they shall not find it. In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst"* (Amos 8:11–13). The famine is not of the word but of hearing it. The bodily thirst comes in the same day.
> 
> Before Samuel, *"the word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision"* (1 Samuel 3:1). The word for *rare* is the word for *precious*. When the call came, the boy did not know it: *"Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him"* (3:7). Three times he ran to Eli, until *"Eli perceived that the Lord was calling the boy"* and taught him the answer, *"Speak, Lord, for your servant hears"* (3:8–9). The old priest, whose eyes were growing dim (3:2), knew the voice the boy could not yet place. I read hearing that had to be learned, in a time when the word was rare.
> 
> Hearing can stop at a single word. Paul tells the crowd of his vision in the temple: *"Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me"* (Acts 22:18). He objected that they knew his past: *"Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you"* (22:19). The answer was *"Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles"* (22:21). Then *"Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live'"* (22:22). They heard him through the persecution and the vision; the word "Gentiles" ended their hearing. Paul had thought his past would make them listen; the Lord had said it would not.
> 
> Ears can be closed to a word that is still being spoken. "To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10). The act is a hearing that does not happen. "Cannot listen" is followed by what they do with the word instead: they scorn it. Taking no pleasure in it is the measure of the scorn. I read the uncircumcised ears as hearing that lacks the mark of belonging to him. The one who must speak is left holding it: "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (6:11).
> 
> Words that are heard can be pictured as tools. The Preacher *"sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth"* (Ecclesiastes 12:10). *"The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd. My son, beware of anything beyond these"* (12:11–12). A goad drives an animal on; a nail holds something in place. I read the figure as two works of the same words on the hearer: they move him, and they fix in him. Delight is in the search for the words, and the words are given by one Shepherd.
> 
> What is heard can also kindle. "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Nehemiah 5:6). And when what is heard lowers the hearers' standing or exposes their guilt, rage can refuse to hear any more. Stephen's hearers "were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him … But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:54, 57). James puts hearing first for this very reason: "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:19–20).
> 
> The same words, read aloud, brought fear to some and none to others. When the scroll of Jeremiah's words was read, the officials "heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king cut it up column by column and burned it, and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments" (36:23–24).
> 
> Understanding can itself be dread: "it will be sheer terror to understand the message" (Isaiah 28:19; Chapter 13). And some hold the word in awe: "Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words" (Psalm 119:161). Section 10.9 follows those who tremble at his word.
> 
> Some things are only understood later. Of God's anger, Jeremiah says, "In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20). Chapter 13 follows how people read, and misread, what has happened to them.
> 
> God also says what knowing him is. Of Josiah: "He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 22:16). It is said against his son, who built "by unrighteousness" and kept back his neighbour's wages (22:13): "But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence" (22:17). Knowing God is named here in a deed done for the poor, and set against a heart and eyes given to gain (10.6).
> 
> Knowing has a beginning, and Scripture names it. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction" (Proverbs 1:7). "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10). To man God said, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding" (Job 28:28). It also runs the other way. The one who seeks wisdom "as for hidden treasures" is told, "then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God" (Proverbs 2:4–5). And it can be refused: "Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 1:29). The fear of God is also learned by hearing (10.9).
> 
> Learning to fear God takes a life. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The ear decides much: "The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise" (Proverbs 15:31). God can open the ear himself. In a dream "he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Delivered from death") gives the setting.
> 
> Wisdom, refused, says: "I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Proverbs 1:26). And "whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster" (1:33).
> 
> What is known is also kept and returned to. Remembering feeds thinking: "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all that you have done; I ponder the work of your hands" (Psalm 143:5).
> 
> Hearing can be woken. "The Lord God has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward" (Isaiah 50:4–5). The order is the verses' own: the ear is woken before the tongue sustains anyone, and it is woken each morning. The next verse goes on to "I gave my back to those who strike" (50:6), so the woken ear is no shelter from suffering. An angel wakes a prophet too, and the first thing said is "What do you see?" (Zechariah 4:1–2; 13.2).
> 
> What is known can be known in heart and soul. Joshua, near death: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed" (Joshua 23:14). This is knowing from experience. He turns it into a warning straight away: "But just as all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (23:15). The faithfulness they know from the good is the same faithfulness that stands behind the warnings.
> 
> Receiving a word can wait on being willing. "and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:14–15). The Bereans "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed" (Acts 17:11–12). Paul calls a saying "trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). The other way is also named: scoffers "following their own sinful desires … deliberately overlook this fact" (2 Peter 3:3, 5). I read the willing, or the unwilling, as standing before the hearing in these verses.

##### Section 385: chapter 10.15 Pride, Pride and hearing

> ## Pride and hearing
> 
> Across all its words, pride is set against hearing.
> - "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jeremiah 13:15). And then: "if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (13:17).
> - "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Proverbs 13:10).
> - The scoffer is known by what he will not receive. He "does not listen to rebuke" (Proverbs 13:1); he "does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). "Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (9:8). The same rebuke meets two hearts. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain" (14:6). When he is struck, others learn: "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25).
> - "Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong … Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isaiah 28:22–23).
> 
> **Presumption** is pride acting on its own word.
> - The prophet "who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak" (Deuteronomy 18:20). Of such a word: "You need not be afraid of him" (18:22).
> - Israel was told, "Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst". "So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the Lord and presumptuously went up into the hill country" (Deuteronomy 1:42–43). It came just after "We have sinned against the Lord. We ourselves will go up" (1:41). I read a presumption that wore the words of repentance and went up when the time to go up had passed.
> - "They and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments … and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them" (Nehemiah 9:16–17). God's answer is in the same breath: "But you are a God ready to forgive" (9:17).
> - The psalmist asks to be kept from it: "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psalm 19:13).
> 
> **God works to keep pride from a person.** "He opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). Paul, given "the surpassing greatness of the revelations", was given a second thing "to keep me from becoming conceited": "a thorn … in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7). The answer to his prayer was "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (12:9).
> 
> What the verses set against pride is hearing, and fear. "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate" (Proverbs 8:13). Section 10.2 takes this up.

##### Section 392: chapter 10.2 Knowing and hearing, Pride and hearing

> ## Pride and hearing
> 
> Pride is set against the ear. "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jeremiah 13:15). The scoffer is known by what he will not hear: he "does not listen to rebuke" (Proverbs 13:1); he "does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (Proverbs 15:12). "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Proverbs 13:10). The word itself can be scorned: "the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn" (Jeremiah 6:10, above). God opens the ear against it: "he opens the ears of men … that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). I read pride as the ear that will not take a word against itself, the opposite of the humility above. The whole account is in 10.15.

##### Verse texts (ESV, from table `verse`)

- Gen 43:30: Then Joseph hurried out, for his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. And he entered his chamber and wept there.
- Exo 2:15: When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.
- Exo 4:24: At a lodging place on the way the Lord met him and sought to put him to death.
- Exo 33:7: Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting. And everyone who sought the Lord would go out to the tent of meeting, which was outside the camp.
- Deu 13:10: You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
- 1Sa 10:21: He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found.
- 1Sa 13:12: I said, ‘ Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the Lord.’ So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering.”
- 1Sa 14:4: Within the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.
- 1Sa 19:10: And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.
- 1Sa 23:14: And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.
- 1Sa 27:4: And when it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he no longer sought him.
- 2Sa 4:8: and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. And they said to the king, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring.”
- 2Sa 12:16: David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground. ^
- 2Sa 17:20: When Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house, they said, “ Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” And the woman said to them, “They have gone over the brook of water.” And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.
- 2Sa 21:1: Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year. And David sought the face of the Lord. And the Lord said, “There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”
- 2Sa 21:2: So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not of the people of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah.
- 1Ki 1:2: Therefore his servants said to him, “Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm.”
- 1Ki 1:3: So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.

##### Observation 14199: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132448_748-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** What it does to those beneath it: Pleading against it before it rises:; Judah: "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" (Gen 44:18). The plea is a long retelling of the father's love (44:19–21 onward); Rachel: "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me" (Gen 31:35). The plea for no anger covers a concealment: she is sitting on the stolen gods (31:34); Reading it as a sign: "If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him" (1Sa 20:7). Saul's anger is to be read as the evidence of Saul's intent. Jonathan's knowledge follows the same path: after the spear, "Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death" (20:33); Anticipating it and scripting a reply: Joab to the messenger: "if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city?' … then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also'" (2Sa 11:20–21). The anger is foreseen, and so is the one sentence that will turn it. That sentence works because the king had wanted Uriah dead. The line manages the king's anger by exposing the king's own secret; Plotting against it from below: "Bigthan and Teresh … became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus" (Est 2:21). This is anger rising from the servants, discovered through Mordecai (2:22); Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32); A group overrules its king: "the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him … 'Send the man back … how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord?'" (1Sa 29:4). The king Achish yields: "Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you" (29:6). The anger comes from suspicion: they fear a loyalty they cannot see.
- **revisit_note:** Captured from _analytics/Clusters/M02 - anger-wrath/wa-cluster-M02-phenomena-v2-20260928.md lines 230-236 (#2305)

##### Observation 15385: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_142827_567-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T14:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** The humble hear what God did for another, and are glad: "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2). David's own deliverance follows: "I sought the Lord, and he answered me" (34:4). The superscription sets it after "he changed his behavior before Abimelech"; "When the humble see it they will be glad" (Psa 69:32). "It" is the deliverance of the speaker, who has said "I am afflicted and in pain" (69:29); I read: in both psalms, one man's boast is in the Lord, not in himself, and the humble are those who are glad at it. Their gladness is at what God did for someone else.

##### Observation 16085: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_152029_065-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T15:22:23Z
- **obs_text:** What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]

- **obs_text:** A heart that is a trap (Ecc 7:26). *"And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her."*: It is the Preacher's own finding, after *"I turned my heart to know and to search out"* (7:25), *"which my soul has sought repeatedly"* (7:28).; The figure is a hunter's: snares and nets for a heart, fetters for hands.; A heart can be a trap set for another person's desire. Escape is tied to "he who pleases God", not to strength of will.

##### Observation 19201: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_164719_204-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:49:06Z
- **obs_text:** Seat.; In the verse: 2Ch 22:9 "heart". The word has a genuine inner-being sense, but the heart is Jehoshaphat's, the dead grandfather's: "who sought the Lord with all his heart". Ahaziah, the one hiding, has no seat. Spurious for this phenomenon (v1 §0). Batch C v3 §7.1 read it as seeking the Lord with the heart. Batch G v3 §16.11 read it as "a dead man honoured for his grandfather's heart". Both readings stand. Neither concerns hiding.; Whose seat: none of the 40 hiders has one. In strand (a) the inner operation belongs to the counsellor, and it is shown by what the counsellor says, not by a seat word (v2, kept above).; Outside the verse — new in v3. In strand (a), the nearest seat word is *nephesh* in its life sense: the life being hunted. David, in the psalm headed by the Ziphites' report that he is "hiding among us" (Psa 54:1), says "the Lord is the upholder of my life" (54:4). The seat word names what is at stake in the hiding, not where the hider feels it. This fits Batch G v3 §5 ("Life spared, life hunted — the *nephesh* as a prize"), which it does not change.; Strand (f), prudence — new in v3: Pro 22:3 ("The prudent sees danger and hides himself") → 22:5 "Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them". The prudent one's hiding is a guarding of the soul. *Nephesh* here is the self that is kept from harm, and it passes the check in that sense. Strand (f) is the only strand of §2 where the one who hides has a seat, and the seat is the thing the hiding protects.

##### Observation 19406: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_165202_414-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:52:11Z
- **obs_text:** Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

- **obs_text:** Jeremiah 8:3: "Death shall be preferred to life": > Q1 citation: ⚠ Check. Ch 2 *Wanting to die*: "Under judgment, death is wished for and withheld". The verse says death "shall be preferred" (H0977, Niphal: *shall be chosen*). "Wished for" softens the choosing word, and "withheld" belongs to Rev 9:6 only, not to Jer 8:3.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: corroborates and adds. Corroborates Ch 2 *Wanting to die*. New: the preference is a choosing word, and the Lord declares it as part of a judgment, after the people had loved, served and gone after other things (v2).; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M25 life/death: carried in Ch 2. M58 evil, M43 declares, M72 hosts: no.; This follows the Topheth judgment (7:30–34). The bones of kings, priests, prophets and people are brought out and spread *"before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped"* (8:2).; Then: *"Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them"* (8:3).; "Preferred" is H0977 in the Niphal: death *shall be chosen* (literal sense of the Niphal) rather than life. The remnant prefer death, and the Lord declares it as part of the judgment.

##### Section 212: chapter 10.9 Relating to God, Waiting, and pleading

> ## Waiting, and pleading
> 
> The soul can speak its hope to itself: "'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him.' The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord" (Lamentations 3:24–26). "Portion" is the word of Psalm 16:5 (10.6). Twice "good" belongs to waiting: the Lord is good to those who wait, and it is good to wait. I read waiting as the place where the soul's hope is put.
> 
> A plea can bring one's own record. Hezekiah, told he would die, "turned his face to the wall and prayed": "Please, O Lord, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And he wept bitterly (Isaiah 38:2–3; 2 Kings 20:2–3). The answer came: "I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life" (Isaiah 38:5). He brought his record. God named his prayer and his tears. I note what the answer names and go no further. Chapter 2 ("Life asked for") has what he wrote afterwards.
> 
> A cry can come only in distress. Of the godless: "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?" (Job 27:9–10). The act asked about is calling on God. I read the questions as setting a cry in distress against calling at all times. Delight in him is named as what would make the difference.
> 
> A plea can end in asking that one's work should last. The prayer of Moses that counts how short a life is (Psalm 90:10, 12) ends: "Return, O Lord! How long? Have pity on your servants!" (Psalm 90:13), "Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us" (90:15), "Let your work be shown to your servants" (90:16), and "Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!" (90:17). "Favor" is the word for pleasantness. What they ask to last is their own work, and they ask it under his favor, beside "your work".
> 
> A plea can come from the poor man's own mouth, and be heard. "I sought the Lord, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears … This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him and saved him out of all his troubles" (Psalm 34:4, 6). "But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high! … For the Lord hears the needy" (Psalm 69:29, 33). The one who calls himself poor is the one who cries, and what he is delivered from includes his fears (10.12).
> 
> A plea can be put to his will alone. "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean" (Matthew 8:2). The man does not doubt the power. He asks the will, and the will answers: "I will; be clean" (8:3; Mark 1:40–41; 13.1).

##### Section 224: chapter 10.10 Relating to others, Fear that arrives with a person

> ### Fear that arrives with a person
> 
> A person's coming can bring fear, because of what it might mean. When Samuel came to Bethlehem, "the elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, 'Do you come peaceably?'" (1 Samuel 16:4). Ahimelech "came to meet David, trembling", and asked, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?" (1 Samuel 21:1). The question each asks shows what they feared.
> 
> Some people carry fear with them because of their power. Of Nebuchadnezzar: "because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed" (Daniel 5:19). The fear followed the power over life and death, and the verse says that power was given by God. Fear can fall on a crowd because of one person: officials "helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them" (Esther 9:3).
> 
> And refusing to be afraid can provoke. When Haman saw Mordecai, "that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (Esther 5:9). The man who would not tremble became the one Haman set out to destroy (5:14).
> 
> Mastery can turn on the day it is hoped for. "on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them", and "the fear of them had fallen on all peoples" (Esther 9:1–2). With no one able to stand against them, the Jews "did as they pleased to those who hated them" (9:5). Before that day, as the edict went out, "many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them" (8:17; 10.12).
> 
> Bathsheba met Adonijah, the brother who had lost the throne, with the same question. "Do you come peacefully?" He said, "Peacefully" (1 Kings 2:13; 10.6).
> 

##### Section 252: chapter 10.12 Fear, Dread laid on others

> ## Dread laid on others
> 
> Fear does not stay with single persons. It falls on peoples and on creatures. In most of these verses God lays it; in Esther no giver is named. The verses say what it led to.
> - "The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth" (Genesis 9:2).
> - "a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob" (Genesis 35:5).
> - "Put them in fear, O Lord! Let the nations know that they are but men!" (Psalm 9:20).
> - "that their hearts may melt, and many stumble. At all their gates I have given the glittering sword" (Ezekiel 21:15). The melting heart is what the sword is given for (*Fear in the body*, above).
> 
> The same dread came to different peoples and ended in different ways.
> - **Rahab:** "as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the Lord your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11).
> - **Moab:** "Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many", and Balak sent for Balaam: "Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me" (Numbers 22:3, 6).
> - **The peoples in Esther's day:** where the king's second edict reached, "there was gladness and joy among the Jews … And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them" (Esther 8:17). The verse gives fear as the only reason. This dread did not send the peoples away, nor set them against the Jews; it brought many of them over to the name of those they feared. On the day itself, "no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples" (9:2; 10.10).
> 
> A people can itself be made a horror to others. "I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (Jeremiah 24:9). "Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds" (Jeremiah 19:8). The feeling is in those who pass by. The verses give the reasons in the people's own deeds: "The Lord could no longer bear your evil deeds" (Jeremiah 44:22). The same root, held by the prophet, is his own grief for them: "dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21).
> 
> One phrase passes through many mouths. Jeremiah gave it as a name: "The Lord does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side" (Jeremiah 20:3). Then he heard it whispered against himself: "For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! 'Denounce him! Let us denounce him!' say all my close friends" (20:10). He answered: "But the Lord is with me as a dread warrior" (20:11). A psalmist heard "the whispering of many" and "terror on every side" (Psalm 31:13), and answered in his own words: "But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God'" (31:14).
> 
> Job's friends say that terrors chase the wicked: "Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels" (Job 18:11). They say it of Job. God's own verdict stands over them: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).

##### Section 390: chapter 10.15 Pride, The other face

> ## The other face
> 
> The same words are not pride when the height is given, or when it faces God.
> - **A heart lifted up in God's ways.** Jehoshaphat "sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments … His heart was courageous in the ways of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:4, 6). The word for "courageous" is the word for Uzziah's heart that "grew proud" (26:16). I read that the lifting is the same and the direction differs.
> - **Strength of soul given.** "On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased" (Psalm 138:3). The word is the one rendered "insolent" in Isaiah 3:5.
> - **A heart not lifted up.** "O Lord, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high … But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother" (Psalm 131:1–2). The arrogant man is "never at rest" (Habakkuk 2:5). The heart that is not lifted up is at rest.
> - **The honour given, and the boast in the Lord** (above).
> 
> Chapter 11 (§4) sets this among the words that change character.
